title: Comprehensive Glossary of Insurance and Life Assurance Terms

blocks.h: This chapter contains more than 600 defined terms drawn from all areas of life insurance theory and practice, Nigerian regulatory frameworks, actuarial science, reinsurance, Insurtech, health insurance, pension products, corporate governance, and the CIIN examination syllabus. Terms are organised into 18 thematic sections rather than a single A–Z list, so that related concepts can be read in context. Each entry provides a concise definition and, where useful, a cross-reference to the chapter where the concept is addressed in depth. Abbreviations appear in their most common form as the headword, with the full form in the definition.
Core doctrines, legal principles, and foundational concepts underpinning all insurance contracts.
Actuarial Risk: The risk that an insurer’s actual claims experience will differ from the mortality, morbidity, or other statistical assumptions used in product pricing and reserving. [Ch. 13]

Adverse Selection: The tendency for individuals with higher-than-average risk to disproportionately seek insurance, because they know their risk level exceeds what the insurer has priced for. Managed through underwriting and group enrolment controls. [Ch. 11]

Aleatory Contract: A contract whose financial outcome depends on an uncertain event; insurance is the classic aleatory contract because the premium is certain but the benefit is conditional on a covered event.
Assignment: The transfer of a policyholder’s rights under an insurance policy to another party; must comply with the terms of the policy and the Insurance Act.
Assured Life: The person on whose life the insurance is effected; the insured. May or may not be the same as the policyholder.
Benefit: The amount payable by the insurer to the beneficiary or policyholder upon the occurrence of a covered event.
Caveat Emptor: Latin for ‘let the buyer beware’. Less applicable in insurance than in commercial contracts due to the insurer’s duty to explain policy terms clearly under NIIRA 2025.
Co-insurance: The sharing of a single large risk among multiple insurers, each accepting a defined percentage of the total coverage. Used for risks that exceed a single insurer’s capacity. [Ch. 18]
Concealment: The deliberate withholding of material facts from the insurer at the time of application. A form of non-disclosure that may entitle the insurer to void the policy.
Consideration: In insurance contract law, the premium paid by the policyholder in exchange for the insurer’s promise of indemnity or benefit.

Contract of Indemnity: An insurance contract that compensates the insured for the actual financial loss suffered, up to the policy limit. Life insurance is generally not an indemnity contract; it pays a fixed sum regardless of actual financial loss.

Contribution: The principle under which, where more than one insurance policy covers the same risk, each insurer contributes proportionally to the total loss. More relevant to general insurance; modified in the life insurance context.

Duty of Disclosure: The obligation of the proposer to disclose all material facts that would influence a prudent insurer in deciding whether to accept the risk and at what terms. Governed by the Insurance Act and modified by NIIRA 2025 to impose a reciprocal duty on insurers. [Ch. 11]
Fortuity: The element of chance or uncertainty that must be present for a risk to be insurable; a loss that is certain to occur is not insurable.
Free Cover: Insurance coverage provided automatically without the need for individual medical underwriting; applies within the Free Cover Limit (FCL) in group life schemes. [Ch. 30]
Frequency (Loss): The number of times a loss event occurs in a defined period within an insurance portfolio; one of the two components of the expected loss (frequency × severity).

Gambling: Distinguished from insurance in that gambling creates a risk that would not otherwise exist (speculative risk), whereas insurance covers an existing risk (pure risk). Insurance is not gambling; the Maysir prohibition in Islamic finance draws this same distinction.
Gross Premium: The total premium paid by the policyholder, comprising the net premium (for pure risk coverage) plus expense and profit loadings.
Gross Written Premium (GWP): Total premiums billed by an insurer to policyholders in a period before any deduction for reinsurance ceded. [Ch. 26]
Inception Date: The date on which insurance coverage commences under a policy.
Indemnity: Restoration to the pre-loss financial position; the principle that insurance should not generate profit for the insured but should only compensate for actual loss.

Insurable Interest: The legal requirement that the policyholder must stand to suffer a financial loss from the occurrence of the insured event. In life insurance, a person has an unlimited insurable interest in their own life and a defined insurable interest in the lives of specified others (spouses, debtors).

Insurance: A mechanism for transferring risk from an individual or organisation to an insurer, in exchange for a premium, whereby the insurer pools many small premiums to pay the larger losses of the few.

Law of Large Numbers: The statistical principle that as the number of independent risk units in an insurance pool increases, the actual loss experience converges toward the expected (average) loss, enabling accurate pricing.
Lapse: The termination of an insurance policy due to non-payment of premium after the expiry of any applicable grace period. [Ch. 11]
Loading: An amount added to the net premium to cover the insurer’s expenses, profit margin, and contingency reserve.
Loss Ratio: Claims incurred as a percentage of premiums earned; the primary measure of underwriting experience. [Ch. 32]
Material Fact: Any fact that would influence a prudent insurer’s decision to accept the risk or the terms on which it would do so.
Maturity Benefit: The sum payable to the policyholder at the end of the policy term under an endowment or savings-linked policy, provided the insured survives to the maturity date.

Moral Hazard: The tendency for the presence of insurance to reduce the insured’s incentive to prevent loss or moderate claims behaviour. Managed through co-payments, deductibles, and claims investigation. [Ch. 32]
Net Premium: The premium required purely to fund expected claims, before any expense or profit loading; the actuarially calculated pure risk premium.
No Premium, No Cover: The fundamental principle that insurance coverage does not commence until the first premium is received; codified in NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 11]
Occurrence Policy: A policy that covers events that occur during the policy period, regardless of when the claim is made. Distinguished from a claims-made policy.
Peril: The specific cause of loss against which insurance is provided (e.g., death, disability, critical illness).
Policy: The written insurance contract between the insurer and the policyholder, setting out the parties’ rights and obligations.
Policyholder: The person or entity who enters into the insurance contract with the insurer and is responsible for paying the premium.
Pool: A collective arrangement under which multiple insurers share a specific category of risk; used for risks that are too large or specialised for individual insurers to cover alone.
Premium: The consideration paid by the policyholder to the insurer in exchange for coverage.
Proposal Form: The application document completed by the proposer seeking insurance, through which material facts are disclosed to the insurer. [Ch. 11]
Proposer: The person who applies for insurance; typically becomes the policyholder if the application is accepted.
Pure Risk: A risk that can only result in loss or no change; it cannot produce a gain. Pure risks are insurable; speculative risks (which can produce either gain or loss) are not.
Reinstatement: The restoration of a lapsed policy to full force, usually on payment of all outstanding premiums and satisfaction of the insurer’s reinstatement underwriting requirements.
Renewal: The continuation of an insurance policy for a further period, typically annually, on payment of the renewal premium.
Representation: A statement made by the proposer to the insurer at the time of application; if materially false, it may entitle the insurer to avoid the policy.
Reserve: Funds held by an insurer to meet future policy obligations (claims reserves, life policy reserves, IBNR provisions). [Ch. 13]
Risk: The possibility that an unfavourable event will occur, resulting in financial loss.
Risk Pooling: The fundamental insurance mechanism: many policyholders contribute premiums to a common fund from which the losses of the few are paid.
Severity (Loss): The magnitude of a single loss event; one of the two components of the expected loss (frequency × severity).
Standard Risk: A policyholder whose risk profile falls within the normal parameters for standard premium rates; neither a substandard risk nor a preferred risk.

Subrogation: The right of the insurer, after paying a claim, to take over the insured’s legal rights to pursue recovery from third parties responsible for the loss. Limited relevance in life insurance but applicable in some accident and liability contexts.
Sum Assured: The defined benefit amount payable under a life insurance policy on occurrence of the covered event.
Surrender: The voluntary termination of a life insurance policy by the policyholder before maturity, typically in exchange for the surrender value.
Surrender Value: The amount payable to the policyholder on voluntary termination of a life insurance policy before its maturity or expiry date. [Ch. 11]
Term: The defined period during which an insurance policy provides coverage.
Uberrimae Fidei: Latin for ‘utmost good faith’. The legal doctrine requiring both parties to an insurance contract to disclose all material information fully and honestly.
Underwriting: The process of assessing a proposed risk and deciding whether to accept it and at what premium and terms. [Ch. 11]
Utmost Good Faith: The obligation on both the insurer and the policyholder to act honestly and disclose all relevant information; the foundation of the insurance contract.
Void Policy: A policy that is treated as never having existed, typically because of a material misrepresentation or non-disclosure by the proposer.
Voidable Policy: A policy that is valid unless and until the insurer exercises its right to avoid it, typically due to non-disclosure discovered after the policy was issued.
Waiting Period: A defined period after policy inception during which certain benefits are not payable; used to manage adverse selection particularly in health insurance. [Ch. 30, 32]

Warranty: A statement of fact in an insurance contract that must be strictly true; breach of warranty entitles the insurer to repudiate the contract, regardless of whether the breach is material to the loss.
Product structures, benefit types, and product-specific terms.
Annuity: A contract under which an insurer pays a periodic income to the annuitant for life (or a defined period) in exchange for a lump sum at the outset. See Retirement Life Annuity. [Ch. 31]
Annuity Rate: The monthly income payable per unit of purchase price; the primary metric for comparing annuity quotations.
Bonus (Reversionary): A guaranteed addition to the sum assured of a with-profits policy, declared annually and once added cannot be removed. [Ch. 10]
Bonus (Terminal): An additional bonus payable at maturity or earlier death on a with-profits policy, in addition to the accumulated reversionary bonuses. [Ch. 10]
Children’s Policy: A life assurance policy taken out on the life of a child, typically to build savings for education or other milestones.
Convertible Term: A term assurance that includes the right to convert to a whole life or endowment policy without further medical evidence at a defined future date.
Credit Life Insurance: Life insurance covering the outstanding balance of a loan in the event of the borrower’s death or total permanent disability, with the lender as beneficiary. [Ch. 30]
Critical Illness Insurance: Insurance paying a lump sum on diagnosis of a specified serious medical condition, provided the insured survives the survival period. [Ch. 32]
Decreasing Term Assurance: Term assurance where the sum assured reduces over the policy term, typically used to cover a repayment mortgage.
Deferred Annuity: A life annuity in which contributions are made during an accumulation phase with income commencing at a future date. [Ch. 31]
Disability Income Insurance: Insurance providing periodic income replacement if the insured becomes unable to work due to illness or injury. Also called income protection insurance. [Ch. 32]
Endowment Policy: A life insurance policy that pays the sum assured on death within the term or on survival to the maturity date, combining protection with savings. [Ch. 10]
Enhanced Annuity: A life annuity paying higher-than-standard income to an annuitant with a diagnosed medical condition reducing life expectancy. [Ch. 31]
Escalating Annuity: A life annuity that increases at a defined rate each year to preserve real purchasing power. [Ch. 31]
Executive Deferred Compensation Arrangement (EDCA): An insurance-backed executive pension plan in which the employer purchases a policy on the executive’s life as deferred compensation. [Ch. 33]
Executive Pension Plan (EPP): An employer-sponsored supplementary pension arrangement for senior executives, bridging the gap between CPS-generated and target retirement income. [Ch. 33]
Family Takaful: The Shari’ah-compliant equivalent of life insurance, providing death and disability protection alongside savings through the PRA/PSA structure. [Ch. 29]
Free-Look Period: A defined period (typically 14–30 days) after policy delivery during which the policyholder may cancel the policy and receive a full premium refund.
Funeral Benefit: A modest fixed sum payable quickly on death to cover immediate funeral expenses. [Ch. 30]
Group Life Insurance: Life insurance covering a defined group (employees) under a single master policy, with each member’s beneficiaries receiving the sum assured on death. [Ch. 30]
Guaranteed Annuity Rate (GAR): A contractual commitment in a deferred annuity to convert the accumulated fund at a defined rate at the deferral date, regardless of future market conditions. [Ch. 31]
Hospital Cash Plan: Insurance paying a fixed daily cash benefit for each day of hospitalisation to compensate for indirect costs. [Ch. 32]
Income Protection Insurance (IPI): Insurance replacing a proportion of the insured’s income during a period of disability caused by illness or injury. [Ch. 32]
Individual Life Assurance: Life insurance on a single insured life, governed by a policy issued to a named policyholder.
Investment-Linked Policy: A policy whose benefits are linked to the market value of underlying investment funds chosen by the policyholder, also called a unit-linked policy. [Ch. 10]
Joint Life Policy: A policy on two or more lives, typically paying the sum assured on the first death. [Ch. 31]

Key Person Insurance: Life or disability insurance on a business key person, with the business as policyholder and beneficiary, protecting against the financial loss from the key person’s death or incapacity. [Ch. 25]
Level Term Assurance: Term assurance with a fixed sum assured throughout the policy term.
Microinsurance: Simple, low-premium, high-volume insurance products designed for low-income populations, typically distributed through community, mobile, or cooperative channels. [Ch. 22]
Mortgage Protection Policy: A life policy designed to repay the outstanding mortgage balance on death or disability of the borrower.
Non-participating Policy: A life policy that does not participate in the insurer’s surplus; benefits are fixed at policy inception.
Paid-Up Policy: A policy on which the policyholder has ceased paying premiums and which continues in force with a reduced sum assured.
Participating Policy (With-Profits): A life policy that participates in the insurer’s distributable surplus through the declaration of reversionary and terminal bonuses. [Ch. 10]
Personal Pension Plan (PPP): A long-term savings and life insurance product for self-employed individuals outside the mandatory CPS. [Ch. 33]
Policy Loan: A loan made by the insurer to the policyholder against the surrender value of an in-force life policy. [Ch. 23]
Retirement Life Annuity (RLA): The immediate life annuity product available under the CPS, providing guaranteed retirement income in exchange for RSA funds. [Ch. 31]
Renewable Term: Term assurance that may be renewed for a further period without evidence of health, at the prevailing premium rates for the attained age.
Single Premium Policy: A policy funded by a single lump-sum premium paid at inception, rather than periodic premiums.
Sum at Risk: The net amount at risk to the insurer: the difference between the sum assured and the policy reserve. [Ch. 13]
Term Assurance: Pure life insurance providing a death benefit only if the insured dies within the defined term; no maturity benefit on survival. [Ch. 10]
Unit-Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP): An insurance product combining life coverage with investment in market-linked unit trust funds. [Ch. 10]
Universal Life: A flexible life insurance product allowing the policyholder to vary the premium and the sum assured within defined limits.
Whole Life Assurance: Life insurance providing permanent death cover with no fixed maturity date, building a cash value over time. [Ch. 10]
With-Profits Policy: See Participating Policy.
Risk assessment, selection, and policy issuance terminology.
Acceptance: The insurer’s decision to provide coverage, either at standard rates or with a rating or exclusion.
Automatic Acceptance Limit: See Free Cover Limit.
Aviation Extra: An additional premium charged for coverage of the risk of death in aviation accidents.
Blood Pressure Loading: A premium loading applied where an applicant’s blood pressure readings indicate elevated cardiovascular mortality risk.
BMI (Body Mass Index): A measure of body weight relative to height used in medical underwriting to assess obesity-related mortality risk.
Census (Group Life): The full schedule of all eligible employees in a group life scheme, containing age, gender, occupation, salary, and sum assured data. [Ch. 30]
Clean (Standard) Risk: An application that presents no adverse risk factors and is accepted at standard premium rates without any loading or exclusion.
Clinical Rating: A premium loading applied in individual underwriting based on a specific medical condition or clinical finding.
Confidential Medical Attendant’s Report (CMAR): A medical report obtained from the applicant’s own doctor, providing the insurer with additional health information.
Counter-Offer: The insurer’s offer to cover a risk on terms different from those applied for; requires the proposer’s acceptance to form a contract.
Decline: The insurer’s refusal to provide coverage, typically because the risk is too high or falls outside the insurer’s appetite.
EFU Life Tables: The Nigerian mortality tables (Experience Follows Up life tables) published for use in life insurance underwriting and pricing. [Ch. 13]

Exclusion: A specific condition, circumstance, or cause of loss that is not covered under the policy. An exclusion may be used instead of a decline where the risk is otherwise acceptable but one element is uninsurable. [Ch. 11]
Faculty Evidence: Medical examination or report required for applicants above the non-medical limit or presenting specific risk factors. [Ch. 11]
Financial Underwriting: Assessment of the financial justification for the level of coverage requested, particularly for large sums assured, to prevent over-insurance.
Free Cover Limit (FCL): The maximum sum assured per member covered in a group scheme without requiring individual medical evidence. [Ch. 30]
Group Underwriting: The assessment of the collective mortality risk of a group of lives, using demographic and claims experience data rather than individual medical evidence. [Ch. 30]
HIV Testing: A standard medical underwriting requirement above defined sum assured thresholds in the Nigerian market, reflecting the impact of HIV/AIDS on life expectancy.
Individual Underwriting: The assessment of the mortality risk of a specific individual through disclosure, medical evidence, and financial analysis. [Ch. 11]
Life Table: A statistical table showing the probability of survival or death at each age, used as the foundation of life insurance underwriting and pricing. [Ch. 13]
Loading (Premium): An additional premium charged above the standard rate to compensate the insurer for a higher-than-average risk. [Ch. 11]
Medical Director: The physician retained by the insurer to advise on medical underwriting decisions and to interpret clinical evidence.
Medical Examination: A clinical examination of an applicant by a NAICOM-approved medical examiner, required above defined sum assured thresholds or for complex risks.
Moral Hazard (Underwriting): The risk that an applicant has concealed information, misrepresented their circumstances, or has an incentive to claim that influenced their application.
Morbidity: The incidence of illness or disability within a population; used in health insurance underwriting and pricing.
Mortality: The statistical frequency of death within a population; the foundational risk concept in life assurance pricing.
Mortality Rate (qx): The probability that a person aged exactly x will die before reaching age x+1, as expressed in a life table.
Non-Medical Limit: The maximum sum assured for which an application may be accepted on the basis of the proposal form alone, without requiring additional medical evidence. [Ch. 11]
Occupation Class: A categorisation of occupations by hazard level used to determine the appropriate premium loading for occupational mortality risk. [Ch. 30]
Occupational Hazard Rating: An additional premium loading applied where the applicant’s occupation is associated with higher-than-average mortality risk. [Ch. 30]
NIGO (Not In Good Order): An application returned to the distributor or agent because it is incomplete, inconsistent, or missing required documentation or signatures.
Proposal Form: The application document through which material facts are disclosed to the insurer. [Ch. 11]
Rating: The application of an additional premium loading to a substandard risk.
Reinsurance Retention Limit: The maximum sum assured that the cedant retains on its own account for any single life risk, above which the excess is ceded to reinsurers. [Ch. 14]
Risk Classification: The categorisation of an applicant’s risk level (standard, substandard, declined) based on the underwriting assessment.

Substandard Risk: An applicant whose risk profile is worse than the standard (e.g., due to health conditions or hazardous occupation) and who is accepted at a higher premium or with exclusions. [Ch. 11]
Treaty: A reinsurance agreement covering a defined class of business automatically, without requiring case-by-case cession. [Ch. 14]
Claims assessment, settlement, and fraud management terminology.
Acknowledgement of Claim: The insurer’s formal confirmation of receipt of a claim notification, required under NIIRA 2025 within 5 business days. [Ch. 12]
Assessor: A professional appointed by the insurer to investigate and evaluate the circumstances and value of a claim.
AWOL (Absent Without Leave): Relevant in military and paramilitary group life claims; a risk that unconfirmed deaths may be claimed while the individual is absent without leave rather than deceased.
Beneficiary: The person or entity designated to receive the death benefit under a life insurance policy. [Ch. 12]
Claim: A formal request by a policyholder or beneficiary for payment of a benefit under an insurance policy. [Ch. 12]
Claims Administration: The complete process of receiving, assessing, approving, and settling insurance claims. [Ch. 12]
Claims Fraud: The deliberate submission of a false or inflated claim to obtain an insurance benefit to which the claimant is not entitled. [Ch. 12]
Claims Incurred But Not Reported (IBNR): An actuarial reserve representing estimated claims that have occurred but have not yet been notified to the insurer. [Ch. 13]
Claims Loss Ratio: Total claims incurred as a percentage of total premium earned; primary health insurance performance measure. [Ch. 32]
Claims Reserve: Funds held by the insurer to pay claims that have been notified but not yet settled, and claims estimated to be incurred but not yet reported. [Ch. 13]
Claims Settlement Time: The period from receipt of complete claims documentation to payment of the benefit; NIIRA 2025 mandates maximum settlement times. [Ch. 12]
Claimant: The person making a claim; may be the policyholder, beneficiary, or legal representative.
Codicil: An addition or amendment to a will; relevant in life insurance claims where the beneficiary designation in the will differs from the policy nomination.
Contested Claim: A claim that the insurer disputes on grounds of non-disclosure, exclusion applicability, or lack of evidence.
Death Certificate: An official document issued by the appropriate civil authority certifying the date, location, and cause of death; primary evidence in death claims. [Ch. 12]
Ex Gratia Payment: A payment made by the insurer as a goodwill gesture without admission of legal liability; used in borderline claims or to resolve disputes.
First Notification of Loss (FNOL): The initial notification by the claimant to the insurer of the occurrence of a potential claim.
Fraud Indicators: Observable characteristics of a claim that suggest potential fraud: inconsistent documentation, unusual timing, multiple policies on the same life, prior history. [Ch. 12]
Good Order Claims: Claims presented with all required documentation, enabling prompt assessment and settlement.

Grant of Probate: The legal authority granted by a court to the executor of a will to administer the deceased’s estate; may be required before a death benefit can be paid where no valid nomination exists.
IBNR: See Claims Incurred But Not Reported.
Interpleader: A legal action by the insurer where competing beneficiaries make conflicting claims to the same benefit, asking the court to determine the rightful claimant.
Letters of Administration: Legal authority granted by a court to an administrator to handle the estate of a person who died intestate (without a will).
Medical Evidence (Claims): Documentation required to substantiate a disability or critical illness claim: hospital records, specialist reports, pathology results. [Ch. 12]
Misrepresentation: A false statement of material fact made by the proposer at application, which may entitle the insurer to avoid the policy.
Mortality Investigation: The analysis of actual deaths within the insurer’s portfolio against the expected mortality from the pricing table; essential input for profit source analysis. [Ch. 13]
Post-Mortem Report: A medical examination report on the cause of death; may be required in accidental death benefit claims where the cause of death is disputed. [Ch. 12]
Proof of Loss: Documentation provided by the claimant substantiating the occurrence and extent of the claimed loss.
Repudiation: The insurer’s formal refusal to pay a claim, typically on grounds of non-disclosure, policy exclusion, or policy lapse. [Ch. 12]
Settlement: The agreed payment resolving a claim between the insurer and the claimant.
Special Investigation Unit (SIU): The unit within the Claims department responsible for investigating claims presenting fraud indicators. [Ch. 12]
Survival Period: The minimum period the insured must survive after a critical illness diagnosis before the CI benefit is payable. [Ch. 32]
Third Party Administrator (TPA): An external company that manages claims on behalf of an insurer, commonly used in group health insurance. [Ch. 32]
Actuarial science concepts, reserving, pricing, and ERM terminology.
Actuarial Assumption: A numerical estimate of a future experience factor (mortality rate, interest rate, lapse rate, expense level) used in life insurance pricing and reserving. [Ch. 13]
Actuarial Certificate: The certification issued by the Statutory Actuary confirming the adequacy of the insurer’s technical provisions, filed with NAICOM annually. [Ch. 13]
Actuarial Investigation (Annual): The annual review by the Statutory Actuary of the insurer’s life business, confirming reserve adequacy and the financial condition of the portfolio. [Ch. 13]

Asset-Liability Management (ALM): The management of assets and liabilities together to minimise the risk of a financial mismatch; particularly important for annuity and long-term life business. [Ch. 23]
Benefit Reserve: The actuarial reserve representing the present value of future benefits less the present value of future premiums; the insurer’s obligation to fund future benefit payments. [Ch. 13]
Credibility: The statistical weight given to an insurer’s own experience data in experience rating, reflecting the volume and reliability of that data. [Ch. 30]
Duration (Investment): The weighted average time to receipt of cash flows from a bond or portfolio; the primary measure of interest rate sensitivity. [Ch. 23]
EFU Life Tables: The mortality tables recommended by NAICOM for use in Nigerian life insurance pricing, based on the experience of insured Nigerian lives. [Ch. 13]
Embedded Value (EV): The present value of shareholders’ interest in a life insurance company: Adjusted Net Asset Value (ANAV) plus Value of In-Force Business (VIF). [Ch. 26]
Experience Rating: A premium rating technique adjusting renewal rates based on the scheme’s own claims history, blended with market expected rates using credibility weighting. [Ch. 30]
Expense Loading: The amount added to the net premium to cover the insurer’s operating expenses. [Ch. 13]
Interest Profit (C2): The profit source arising from the difference between the assumed and actual investment return on the policy reserve. [Ch. 26]
Lapse Profit (C4): The profit source arising from the difference between assumed and actual lapse rates. [Ch. 26]
Liability Adequacy Test (LAT): An IFRS 17 requirement to confirm that the insurer’s insurance contract liabilities are sufficient to cover future cash outflows. [Ch. 24]
Life Expectancy: The expected number of additional years of life remaining for a person of a given age, calculated from a mortality table. [Ch. 31]
Longevity Risk: The risk that annuitants live longer than the mortality assumption, requiring more years of annuity payments than priced for. [Ch. 31]
Mortality Improvement Factors: Projections of the expected annual rate of improvement in mortality rates, incorporated into annuity pricing and reserving. [Ch. 31]
Mortality Profit (C1): The profit source arising from the difference between assumed and actual mortality experience. [Ch. 26]
New Business Margin (NBM): New Business Value divided by Present Value of New Business Premium; the primary metric of new business profitability. [Ch. 26]
New Business Value (NBV): The present value of future shareholder profits from policies written in the current period. [Ch. 26]
ORSA (Own Risk and Solvency Assessment): The insurer’s annual self-assessment of its risk profile, risk appetite, and capital adequacy, required under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 15]
Policy Reserve: Funds held by the insurer to meet its future obligations under in-force life policies. [Ch. 13]
Present Value: The current worth of future cash flows, discounted at an appropriate interest rate. [Ch. 13]
Profit Source Analysis: The decomposition of life insurance profit into mortality (C1), interest (C2), expense (C3), and lapse (C4) components. [Ch. 26]
Pure Premium: The net premium required solely to fund expected claims, without any expense or profit loading.
Risk Discount Rate: The rate used to discount future profits in embedded value calculations, reflecting the required return on the capital supporting the life business. [Ch. 26]

Risk-Based Capital (RBC): A capital requirement framework that links the minimum capital the insurer must hold to its specific risk profile, replacing the traditional fixed-percentage solvency margin. [Ch. 15]
Solvency Margin: The excess of an insurer’s assets over its liabilities; the financial buffer protecting policyholders. [Ch. 24]
Statutory Actuary: The Fellow of a recognised actuarial institute responsible for certifying the annual actuarial investigation, with a direct reporting line to the Board under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 13]
Stress Testing: The evaluation of an insurer’s financial resilience by applying severe but plausible adverse scenarios to its balance sheet and income statement. [Ch. 15]
Value of In-Force Business (VIF): The present value of future after-tax shareholder profits expected from the existing in-force policy portfolio. [Ch. 26]
Reinsurance structures, markets, and cession terminology.

Automatic Treaty: A reinsurance agreement under which the cedant is obligated to cede, and the reinsurer is obligated to accept, all business meeting defined criteria, without case-by-case facultative placement. [Ch. 14]
Capacity: The maximum amount of risk a reinsurer (or insurer) is willing and able to accept.
Cat XL (Catastrophe Excess of Loss): A reinsurance cover responding when aggregate claims from a single catastrophic event exceed a defined retention. [Ch. 30]
Cedant: The insurer that cedes (transfers) risk to a reinsurer. [Ch. 14]
Cession: The portion of risk (and corresponding premium) transferred from the cedant to the reinsurer. [Ch. 14]
Commutation: The termination of a reinsurance treaty, typically involving a lump-sum payment to settle all outstanding obligations.
Continental Reinsurance (Continental Re): A major Nigerian-based pan-African reinsurer providing proportional and non-proportional reinsurance capacity to Nigerian cedants. [Ch. 14]

Domestic Cession Requirement: The obligation of Nigerian insurers under NIIRA 2025 to offer a defined proportion of their reinsurance to domestic reinsurers before placing with international markets. [Ch. 14]
Excess of Loss (XL) Treaty: A non-proportional reinsurance arrangement under which the reinsurer pays the portion of a loss exceeding the cedant’s retention. [Ch. 14]

Facultative Reinsurance: Case-by-case reinsurance placement, negotiated individually for specific large or unusual risks; the cedant is not obligated to cede and the reinsurer is not obligated to accept. [Ch. 14]
Follow the Fortunes: A reinsurance doctrine requiring the reinsurer to follow the cedant’s fortunes in claims settlement, provided the cedant acts in good faith and within the treaty terms.
Fronting: An arrangement under which a licensed insurer issues a policy but cedes 100% of the risk to an unlicensed party; generally prohibited under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 14]
Inward Reinsurance: Reinsurance accepted by a company from other insurers or reinsurers; the company acts as a reinsurer.
Line (Reinsurance): The maximum amount a reinsurer will accept on a single risk under a treaty.
Net Retention: The amount of risk the cedant retains on its own account after cession to reinsurers. [Ch. 14]
Nigerian Reinsurance Corporation (NRC): A federal government-linked reinsurance company providing domestic reinsurance capacity; part of the domestic cession obligation market. [Ch. 14]
Outward Reinsurance: Reinsurance ceded by an insurer to reinsurers to reduce its net exposure.
Proportional Treaty: A reinsurance structure (quota share or surplus) in which premiums and losses are shared in defined proportions. [Ch. 14]
Quota Share: A proportional reinsurance treaty under which the cedant cedes a fixed percentage of all premiums and losses across a defined class of business. [Ch. 14]
Re-Takaful: The Takaful equivalent of reinsurance, structured on Shari’ah-compliant mutual contribution principles. [Ch. 29]
Reinsurance Broker: An intermediary who arranges reinsurance placements on behalf of cedants; regulated under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 14]
Reinsurance Commission: The commission paid by the reinsurer to the cedant under a proportional treaty, compensating the cedant for its acquisition and administration expenses. [Ch. 14]
Reinsurance Recovery: The amount recovered by the cedant from reinsurers in respect of a ceded claim.
Reinsurance Treaty: The master reinsurance agreement between the cedant and reinsurer, setting out the terms under which risks are ceded and recovered. [Ch. 14]
Retention: The net amount of risk the cedant keeps on its own account; defined in the treaty as a retention limit (per life or per event) or a retention percentage. [Ch. 14]
Slip: The document summarising the key terms of a facultative reinsurance placement, initialled by each reinsurer to indicate their acceptance of a line.
Surplus Treaty: A proportional treaty under which the cedant retains a defined line (fixed sum) and cedes the surplus above the retained line. [Ch. 14]
Technical Account (Reinsurance): The insurer’s reinsurance result: premiums ceded minus claims recovered.
Unearned Premium Reserve (UPR): The portion of written premium relating to future coverage periods; must be ceded to reinsurers in proportion to the cession ratio. [Ch. 26]
Yearly Renewable Term (YRT): A group life reinsurance structure under which the cedant retains the first defined amount of each individual claim and cedes the excess. [Ch. 30]
Investment management, financial reporting, and portfolio terminology.
Admissible Assets: Assets that qualify for inclusion in the insurer’s solvency margin calculation under NAICOM’s admissible asset framework. [Ch. 23]
ALCO (Asset-Liability Committee): The committee responsible for oversight of the insurer’s ALM strategy, typically comprising the CEO, CFO, CIO, and Statutory Actuary. [Ch. 23]
Annual Management Charge (AMC): The annual percentage of fund value deducted from a unit-linked policy to cover investment management and administration costs. [Ch. 33]
Asset Allocation: The division of an investment portfolio among different asset classes (equities, bonds, real estate, money market) in defined proportions. [Ch. 23]
Bond Duration: The weighted average time to receipt of bond cash flows; the primary measure of the bond’s price sensitivity to interest rate changes. [Ch. 23]
Capital Adequacy: The requirement that an insurer hold sufficient capital (assets in excess of liabilities) to absorb unexpected losses and protect policyholders. [Ch. 24]
Corporate Bond: A fixed-income security issued by a corporation, offering higher yield than government bonds but with credit risk. [Ch. 23]
Credit Rating: An independent assessment of the creditworthiness of a bond issuer or debt instrument, expressed as a letter grade (e.g., AAA, AA, B). [Ch. 23]
Default Risk: The risk that a bond issuer fails to make the scheduled interest or principal payment. [Ch. 23]
Dividend: A distribution of profits by a company to its shareholders; a component of equity investment return. [Ch. 23]

Duration Gap: The difference between the duration of the insurer’s assets and the duration of its liabilities; a positive gap means assets are shorter-dated than liabilities, creating reinvestment risk. [Ch. 23]

FGN Bond (Federal Government of Nigeria Bond): A sovereign debt security issued by the FGN through the Debt Management Office; the primary fixed-income admissible asset for Nigerian insurers. [Ch. 23]
Fund Manager: An investment professional responsible for making investment decisions for a defined portfolio.
Impairment: A reduction in the carrying value of an investment asset to reflect a permanent or significant decline in its fair value.
Investment Policy Statement (IPS): The Board-approved document defining the insurer’s investment objectives, risk tolerance, asset allocation strategy, and prohibited instruments. [Ch. 23]
Investment Yield: Total investment income as a percentage of average invested assets; the primary measure of the portfolio’s income-generating efficiency. [Ch. 26]
Liquidity Risk: The risk that the insurer cannot convert assets to cash quickly enough to meet its claims and operational obligations. [Ch. 23]
Mark-to-Market: The valuation of investment assets at their current market price, rather than historical cost. [Ch. 23]
Net Earned Premium (NEP): Net written premium adjusted for the change in unearned premium reserve. [Ch. 26]
Net Written Premium (NWP): Gross written premium minus reinsurance premium ceded. [Ch. 26]
Policy Loan: A loan made by the insurer to a policyholder, secured against the surrender value of an in-force life policy. [Ch. 23]
Portfolio Yield: See Investment Yield.
Premium Income: Total premiums received from policyholders in a defined period. [Ch. 26]
Real Estate Investment: Direct or indirect investment in property as part of the insurer’s investment portfolio; an admissible asset class under NAICOM guidelines. [Ch. 23]
Reinvestment Risk: The risk that, when a bond matures, the reinvested proceeds earn a lower rate than the original bond. [Ch. 23]
Solvency Ratio: The insurer’s actual capital as a percentage of the required minimum capital under the applicable solvency framework. [Ch. 24]
Sukuk: An Islamic bond structured around asset-backed returns rather than interest payments; a key Shari’ah-compliant investment instrument for Takaful funds. [Ch. 29]
Technical Provisions: The liabilities of an insurer relating to its insurance contracts, including the policy reserve, claims reserves, and other actuarial provisions. [Ch. 13]
Treasury Bill (T-Bill): A short-term government debt instrument with maturity of one year or less; the primary money market instrument for Nigerian insurers. [Ch. 23]
Unrealised Gain/Loss: The increase or decrease in the market value of an investment that has not yet been converted to cash through a sale. [Ch. 23]
Nigerian insurance regulatory framework, NAICOM powers, and NIIRA 2025 provisions.
Approved Securities: Investment instruments specifically approved by NAICOM for inclusion in an insurer’s solvency margin calculation. [Ch. 23]

AML/CFT: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism; the regulatory framework requiring insurers to implement KYC, transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting under the MLPPA 2022. [Ch. 21]
Class of Insurance: A defined category of insurance business (life, non-life, composite) for which a separate NAICOM licence is required.
Combined Code of Corporate Governance: The Nigerian Code of Corporate Governance 2018 issued by the FRC, setting governance standards for public interest entities including listed insurers. [Ch. 34]

Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020: The primary Nigerian corporate law, governing company formation, directors’ duties, and annual reporting requirements for all registered companies. [Ch. 34]

Consumer Protection Bureau (NAICOM): The NAICOM division responsible for handling policyholder complaints, monitoring market conduct, and enforcing the consumer protection provisions of NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 21]
Fit and Proper Requirement: NAICOM’s standards for directors and key management personnel: qualifications, experience, integrity, and absence of disqualifying conduct. [Ch. 34]
GAID 2025 (General Application and Implementation Directive): The directive implementing the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 for data controllers and processors, effective September 2025. [Ch. 21]
Gazette: The Federal Government’s official publication for statutory instruments, regulations, and official notices; NAICOM uses the Gazette to issue legally binding circulars. [Ch. 21]
Gross Premium Ratio Method: A method of calculating the minimum solvency margin based on a percentage of gross written premium. [Ch. 24]
IFRS 17: International Financial Reporting Standard 17 (Insurance Contracts), the accounting standard for insurance contracts effective for Nigerian listed insurers, replacing IFRS 4. [Ch. 24]
Insurance Levy: The annual regulatory levy paid by licensed insurers to NAICOM, calculated as a percentage of gross premium income. [Ch. 21]
Insurance Ombudsman: A proposed alternative dispute resolution mechanism for policyholder complaints under NIIRA 2025, providing a faster and less costly route than formal litigation. [Ch. 21]

Insurtech Guidelines (NAICOM 2025): NAICOM’s regulatory framework for technology-driven insurance innovations, including the Partnering Insurtech and Standalone Insurtech licensing tracks and the regulatory sandbox. [Ch. 28]
KYC (Know Your Customer): The process of verifying the identity and risk profile of policyholders and other business relationships, required under the MLPPA 2022 and NAICOM AML guidelines. [Ch. 21]
Licence: The NAICOM authorisation permitting a company to transact a defined class of insurance business in Nigeria. [Ch. 21]
Market Conduct: The behaviour of insurers and their agents toward policyholders and prospective customers; regulated by NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework. [Ch. 21]
Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR): The minimum paid-up capital prescribed by NIIRA 2025 for licensed insurers; the threshold for initial and ongoing licensing. [Ch. 24]
MLPPA 2022: The Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022; the primary Nigerian AML/CFT legislation applicable to insurers. [Ch. 21]
NAICOM: The National Insurance Commission; the apex regulator of the insurance industry in Nigeria, established under the NAICOM Act 1997 and with enhanced powers under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 21]
NAICOM Act 1997: The legislation establishing NAICOM as Nigeria’s insurance regulator, now read together with NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 21]

NDPA 2023 (Nigeria Data Protection Act): The primary data protection legislation applicable to Nigerian insurers as data controllers, imposing obligations on consent, data minimisation, breach notification, and data subject rights. [Ch. 21]

NIIRA 2025 (Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025): The Act No. 2 of 2025 that consolidates and replaces the Insurance Act 2003, introducing RBC, Insurtech licensing, enhanced consumer protection, and updated capital requirements. The foundational regulatory instrument for this work. [Ch. 21]

No Objection Certificate: A NAICOM-issued approval authorising a specific transaction or arrangement (e.g., a change of ownership, a reinsurance arrangement) that requires prior NAICOM approval. [Ch. 21]
Non-life Insurance: Insurance other than life assurance; includes property, casualty, marine, motor, and aviation insurance; regulated by NAICOM under a separate licence class.
Paid-Up Capital: The amount of share capital actually received from shareholders; used as the basis for the minimum capital requirement under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 24]
Product Approval: NAICOM’s review and approval of an insurer’s proposed new product before it can be marketed; governed by the NAICOM product approval guidelines. [Ch. 21]
Recapitalisation: The process of increasing an insurer’s paid-up capital to meet NIIRA 2025’s new minimum capital requirements. [Ch. 24]
Regulatory Sandbox: The NAICOM framework allowing Insurtech companies to test innovative insurance models under controlled supervision before full licensing. [Ch. 28]
Run-Off: The managed wind-down of an insurer’s portfolio of obligations after it has ceased writing new business. [Ch. 33]
Statutory Return: The annual regulatory filing submitted by a licensed insurer to NAICOM, including financial statements, actuarial report, and market conduct data. [Ch. 24]
Supervision: NAICOM’s ongoing monitoring of licensed insurers’ financial soundness, governance, and market conduct. [Ch. 21]

Treating Customers Fairly (TCF): The NIIRA 2025 regulatory principle requiring insurers to ensure their products, distribution, servicing, and claims management genuinely deliver fair outcomes to policyholders. [Ch. 21]
Insurance distribution channels, agents, brokers, and bancassurance.
Agency Force: The collective body of tied agents appointed by an insurer to sell its products. [Ch. 17]
Agent: An individual licensed by NAICOM to sell insurance products on behalf of one or more licensed insurers. [Ch. 17]
AFYP (Annualised First Year Premium): The total first-year premium from new policies written in a period, annualised to a 12-month basis regardless of the premium frequency. [Ch. 17]
Bancassurance: The distribution of insurance products through a bank’s existing customer network and branch infrastructure. [Ch. 16]
Broker: An intermediary who acts on behalf of the client (not the insurer) to source and place insurance coverage, regulated under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 18]
Brokerage: The commission earned by a broker for placing insurance on behalf of a client; distinct from agent commission in that it is paid to an intermediary acting for the buyer. [Ch. 18]
CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost): The total cost incurred to acquire one new policyholder, including marketing, agent commission, and underwriting costs. [Ch. 20]
Cold Calling: Unsolicited contact with prospective customers; regulated under NIIRA 2025 and NDPA 2023 to protect consumers from aggressive marketing. [Ch. 21]
Commission: Remuneration paid by the insurer to an agent or broker for placing insurance business. [Ch. 17]
Commission Clawback: The recovery by the insurer of first-year commission from an agent when a policy lapses within a defined early period. [Ch. 35]
Conservation: The process of preventing policy lapses through proactive outreach to at-risk policyholders. [Ch. 20]
Conversion Rate: The proportion of leads or prospects that result in issued policies; a key digital channel distribution metric. [Ch. 28]
Corporate Agent: A company licensed to distribute insurance products on behalf of a licensed insurer; includes banks (bancassurance), fintech companies, and other platform businesses. [Ch. 16]
Cross-Selling: Offering additional insurance products to existing policyholders based on their profile and existing coverage. [Ch. 20]
Digital Corporate Agent: A company holding a NAICOM corporate agent licence that distributes insurance through a digital platform. [Ch. 28]
Direct Response: Insurance sold directly by the insurer to the customer without an intermediary, typically through advertising, mail, telephone, or digital channels. [Ch. 16]
Distribution Channel: The mechanism through which insurance products are sold to customers: tied agent, bancassurance, broker, direct, digital, embedded. [Ch. 16]
Embedded Insurance: Insurance integrated into a non-insurance product or transaction, automatically activated at the point of the primary transaction. [Ch. 28]
Field Force: See Agency Force.
First-Year Commission (FYC): Commission paid to an agent on the first-year premium of a new policy. [Ch. 17]
Free Look Period: The period after policy delivery during which the policyholder may cancel without penalty. [Ch. 11]
Insurance Agent: See Agent.
Intermediary: Any person or company that facilitates the sale of insurance between an insurer and a policyholder; includes agents and brokers. [Ch. 16]
Lead: A prospective customer who has expressed interest in or been identified as a potential buyer of an insurance product. [Ch. 19]
Lapse Rate: The proportion of in-force policies that terminate (lapse) in a defined period, typically measured at 13 months. [Ch. 11]
NPS (Net Promoter Score): A customer loyalty metric based on the proportion of customers who would recommend the insurer’s products and services to others. [Ch. 20]
Overriding Commission: Commission paid by the insurer to an agency manager or unit manager on the production of the agents in their unit. [Ch. 17]
Persistency: The proportion of policies in force that remain active at a defined anniversary (typically 13 months); the inverse of lapse rate. [Ch. 11]
Proposal Form: The application form completed by the proposer, disclosing the information required for underwriting. [Ch. 11]
Referral: A recommendation by an existing customer or professional contact directing a prospective customer to the insurer or agent. [Ch. 20]
Renewal Commission: Commission paid to an agent on the renewal premium of an in-force policy in subsequent years. [Ch. 17]
Suitability: The requirement under NIIRA 2025 that the product or advice provided must be genuinely appropriate for the client’s specific circumstances, needs, and risk tolerance. [Ch. 21]
Tied Agent: An agent who sells the products of a single insurer only, as opposed to an independent or multi-insurer agent. [Ch. 17]
Unit Manager: A manager responsible for a team of tied agents within the insurer’s field sales structure. [Ch. 17]
USSD Insurance: Insurance distribution through Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD) codes on mobile phones, enabling policy purchase without internet access. [Ch. 28]

blocks.title: Section 10: Risk Management and Enterprise Risk Management (ERM)

blocks.h: ERM frameworks, risk appetite, and risk categories applicable to life insurers.
Catastrophe Risk: The risk of an extreme event generating losses many multiples above normal expectations (pandemic, earthquake, workplace disaster). [Ch. 15]
Concentration Risk: The risk of excessive exposure to a single counterparty, asset class, geographic area, or product line. [Ch. 15]
Contagion Risk: The risk that difficulties in one institution or market spread to others, including the insurer’s own operations. [Ch. 15]
Credit Risk: The risk of loss arising from the failure of a counterparty (bond issuer, bank, reinsurer) to meet its financial obligations. [Ch. 15]
Cybersecurity Risk: The risk of unauthorised access to the insurer’s systems, data exfiltration, ransomware, or service disruption. [Ch. 28]
ERM (Enterprise Risk Management): A structured, comprehensive approach to identifying, assessing, managing, monitoring, and reporting all material risks across an organisation. [Ch. 15]
Group Risk: The risk arising from the insurer’s membership of a group of companies, including contagion from group financial difficulties and governance risks. [Ch. 15]
Insurance Risk: The risk of loss arising from the insurer’s underwriting activities: adverse mortality, morbidity, longevity, lapse, or expense experience. [Ch. 15]
Interest Rate Risk: The risk of loss arising from adverse movements in interest rates, particularly for long-duration liabilities such as annuities and endowments. [Ch. 15]
Liquidity Risk: The risk that the insurer cannot convert assets to cash quickly enough to meet its claims and operational payments. [Ch. 15]
Market Risk: The risk of loss from adverse movements in market prices (interest rates, equity prices, property values, exchange rates). [Ch. 15]
Model Risk: The risk that an AI or ML model produces incorrect outputs due to flawed development, poor data quality, or changed conditions. [Ch. 28]
Operational Risk: The risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, or systems, or from external events. [Ch. 15]
ORSA (Own Risk and Solvency Assessment): The insurer’s annual self-assessment of its risk profile, risk appetite, and capital adequacy, required under NIIRA 2025. [Ch. 15]
Pandemic Risk: The risk that a widespread disease event significantly increases mortality claims across the insurer’s life portfolio simultaneously. [Ch. 15]
Regulatory Risk: The risk of loss or constraint arising from changes in the regulatory framework, NAICOM enforcement action, or regulatory non-compliance. [Ch. 15]
Residual Risk: The remaining level of risk after controls and mitigation measures have been applied. [Ch. 15]
Risk Appetite: The level and types of risk an insurer is willing to accept in pursuit of its strategic objectives. [Ch. 15]
Risk Appetite Statement (RAS): The Board-approved document articulating the insurer’s risk appetite across all material risk categories. [Ch. 15]
Risk Heat Map: A visual tool displaying risks by their likelihood and potential impact, enabling prioritisation of risk management attention. [Ch. 15]
Risk Limit: A specific quantitative boundary on an individual risk within the overall risk appetite (e.g., maximum single-name credit exposure). [Ch. 15]
Risk Owner: The individual responsible for managing a specific risk within the ERM framework. [Ch. 15]
Risk Register: The comprehensive record of all identified material risks, their assessments, owners, and mitigation actions. [Ch. 15]
Scenario Analysis: The evaluation of the insurer’s financial position under defined hypothetical scenarios; input to the ORSA. [Ch. 15]
Strategic Risk: The risk that the insurer’s strategy is fundamentally flawed or that execution is so poor that strategic objectives are not achieved. [Ch. 27]

Three Lines of Defence: The governance model in which operational management (1st line) owns risk; Risk and Compliance (2nd line) designs the framework; Internal Audit (3rd line) provides independent assurance. [Ch. 34]
Technology, digital distribution, AI, and data terms in insurance.
AI (Artificial Intelligence): The simulation of human intelligence by computer systems; applied in insurance for underwriting, fraud detection, and claims processing. [Ch. 28]
Algorithm: A defined set of rules or instructions for solving a problem or making a decision; used in automated underwriting and risk scoring.
Alternative Data: Data generated by digital behaviour (mobile money transactions, airtime usage, geolocation) used to supplement traditional underwriting data. [Ch. 28]
API (Application Programming Interface): A set of protocols enabling two software systems to communicate and exchange data; the technical foundation of embedded insurance integration. [Ch. 28]
Automated Underwriting: A rules-based or AI-powered system making underwriting decisions without human intervention for standard risk applications. [Ch. 28]
Big Data: Very large datasets requiring specialised tools to process and analyse; used in insurance for risk pricing, fraud detection, and customer analytics. [Ch. 28]
Blockchain: A distributed, tamper-evident ledger maintained by multiple network participants; used in parametric insurance and reinsurance settlement. [Ch. 28]
Bot / Chatbot: An automated conversational programme; used in insurance for first-level customer service, claims notification, and policy queries. [Ch. 28]

Cloud Computing: The delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, software) over the internet; enabling more scalable and cost-efficient technology infrastructure for insurers. [Ch. 28]
Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): The total cost to acquire a new policyholder, including digital marketing, platform costs, and any commission paid to digital partners. [Ch. 28]
Cybersecurity: The practice of protecting computer systems and data from unauthorised access, theft, and disruption. [Ch. 28]
Data Analytics: The systematic analysis of data to identify patterns, draw conclusions, and support decision-making. [Ch. 28]
Data Governance: The framework of policies, processes, and accountability for managing data assets in compliance with NDPA 2023 and other requirements. [Ch. 28]
Digital Distribution: The use of digital channels (mobile app, USSD, website, embedded API) as the primary or supplementary mechanism for reaching insurance customers. [Ch. 28]
Digital Insurer: See Full-Stack Digital Insurer.
Embedded Insurance: Insurance integrated into a non-insurance product or transaction. [Ch. 28]
Fintech: Financial technology; technology companies providing financial services, typically in banking, payments, and lending.
Full-Stack Digital Insurer: A company holding its own insurance licence and operating the complete insurance value chain through digital infrastructure. [Ch. 28]
Insurtech: The application of technology to improve the efficiency, accessibility, and personalisation of insurance products and services. [Ch. 28]
IoT (Internet of Things): The network of physical devices embedded with sensors that collect and transmit data; used in parametric trigger monitoring and telematics. [Ch. 28]
Lapse Prediction Model: An AI/ML model identifying at-risk policyholders based on behavioural signals to enable targeted conservation. [Ch. 28]
Machine Learning (ML): A subset of AI in which systems learn from data to improve performance without being explicitly programmed. [Ch. 28]
Model Risk: The risk that an AI/ML model produces incorrect or biased outputs; requires ongoing monitoring and validation. [Ch. 28]
NDPA 2023: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023; the primary data protection law applicable to insurers as data controllers. [Ch. 21]
Open Banking/API: The sharing of financial data between institutions through open APIs, enabling new product innovations and embedded insurance.
Oracle (Blockchain): A trusted external data source delivering real-world data (weather, commodity prices) to a blockchain smart contract for parametric trigger verification. [Ch. 28]

Parametric Insurance: Insurance that pays a defined benefit automatically when a measurable index (rainfall, wind speed) reaches a trigger level, without requiring individual loss assessment. [Ch. 28]
PAS (Policy Administration System): The core software system managing an insurer’s policy records, premium transactions, claims, and customer data. [Ch. 34]
RPA (Robotic Process Automation): Software robots that automate repetitive rule-based processes such as data entry, report generation, and premium reconciliation. [Ch. 28]
Sandbox (Regulatory): NAICOM’s controlled environment for testing innovative insurance models under supervision before full licensing. [Ch. 28]
Smart Contract: A self-executing programme on a blockchain that automatically implements agreement terms when predefined conditions are met. [Ch. 28]
Telematics: Technology that collects real-time data on the behaviour of an insured asset (vehicle, person) for pricing and monitoring. [Ch. 28]
USSD: Unstructured Supplementary Service Data; a mobile communication protocol enabling insurance services without internet access. [Ch. 28]
Virtual Agent: An AI-powered digital assistant that performs agent-like functions (lead qualification, needs analysis, product recommendation) without a human agent. [Ch. 16]
Insurance law, policy interpretation, and contractual rights terminology.
Affidavit: A sworn written statement used as evidence in legal and claims proceedings.
Assignment (Policy): The transfer of a policyholder’s rights under an insurance policy to another party, subject to the insurer’s acceptance.
Attestation Clause: The clause in a will certifying that the will was properly signed and witnessed.
Beneficiary Designation: The policyholder’s formal designation of who will receive the death benefit. [Ch. 25]
Binding Authority: Authority granted to a coverholder or managing agent to enter into insurance contracts on behalf of the insurer.
BOI Order: A court order by a Beneficiary of Interests; may affect the distribution of a death benefit where the policyholder’s estate is involved.
CAMA 2020: Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020; the primary corporate governance legislation for Nigerian companies. [Ch. 34]
Capacity (Legal): The legal ability of a person to enter into an insurance contract; minors may not enter into insurance contracts in their own right.
Certificate of Insurance: A document certifying that an insurance policy is in force, typically issued to third parties as evidence of coverage. [Ch. 30]
Claim Form: The standardised document completed by a claimant to initiate an insurance claim. [Ch. 12]
Commencement Date: The date on which an insurance policy becomes effective.
Conditions: The terms and obligations in an insurance policy that must be met by the policyholder to maintain coverage.
Consumer Protection: The regulatory framework protecting policyholders from unfair practices by insurers and intermediaries. [Ch. 21]
Contra Proferentem: A legal doctrine requiring ambiguous insurance policy terms to be interpreted against the party that drafted them (the insurer). [Ch. 11]
Contestability Period: The period (typically the first 1–2 years of a policy) during which the insurer may investigate and potentially deny a claim based on material misrepresentation. [Ch. 11]
Days of Grace: See Grace Period.
Disclosure: The obligation of the proposer to reveal all material facts to the insurer at the time of application. [Ch. 11]
Endorsement: A written amendment to an insurance policy, modifying the original terms. [Ch. 11]
Exclusion Clause: A policy provision specifying circumstances or risks that are not covered. [Ch. 11]
Express Terms: Terms that are explicitly stated in the insurance policy document.
Fraud: Deliberate deception by the insured to obtain a benefit to which they are not entitled. [Ch. 12]
Grace Period: A defined period after the premium due date during which a premium may be paid without the policy lapsing. [Ch. 11]
Implied Terms: Terms that are not explicitly stated in the policy but are implied by law or by the nature of the contract.
Indisputable Clause: See Incontestability Clause.

Incontestability Clause: A policy provision stating that after a defined period (typically 2 years), the insurer cannot contest the policy on grounds of misrepresentation, except in cases of fraud. [Ch. 11]
Insurable Interest: The legal requirement that the policyholder must have a financial interest in the subject matter of the insurance. [Ch. 11]
Insurance Contract: The legal agreement between the insurer and the policyholder setting out rights and obligations. [Ch. 11]
Intestacy: The legal situation arising when a person dies without a valid will; the distribution of their estate is governed by applicable inheritance law. [Ch. 25]
Letter of Administration: Legal authority granted by a court to administer the estate of a person who died intestate. [Ch. 12]
Misrepresentation: A false statement of a material fact in the insurance application. [Ch. 11]
Nomination of Beneficiary: The formal designation of who will receive the policy benefit on death. [Ch. 25]
Non-Disclosure: The failure to reveal a material fact to the insurer at the time of application. [Ch. 11]
Offer and Acceptance: The basic contract formation mechanism; in insurance, the proposal form is typically the offer and the insurer’s acceptance letter or cover note is the acceptance.
Operative Clause: The main insuring clause of the policy, defining the insurer’s primary obligation.
Premium Clause: The policy clause specifying the premium amount, frequency, and payment terms. [Ch. 11]
Probate: The legal process of proving the validity of a will and authorising the executor to administer the estate. [Ch. 25]
Repudiation: The insurer’s refusal to be bound by a claim or the policy. [Ch. 12]
Rescission: The cancellation of a contract, returning both parties to their original positions. [Ch. 11]
Schedule: The part of the policy document setting out the specific details of the coverage (insured name, sum assured, premium, effective date). [Ch. 11]
Subrogation: The insurer’s right to pursue recovery from third parties after paying a claim.
Trust: A legal arrangement in which assets are held by a trustee for the benefit of beneficiaries; used in life insurance for estate planning. [Ch. 25]
Warranty (Insurance): A term in an insurance contract that must be strictly true; a strict condition of coverage. [Ch. 11]

blocks.title: Section 13: Takaful and Islamic Finance Terms

blocks.h: Shari’ah-compliant insurance and Islamic finance terminology.
AAOIFI: Accounting and Auditing Organisation for Islamic Financial Institutions; the primary global standard-setter for Shari’ah compliance in Takaful and Islamic finance. [Ch. 29]
Darurah: The Islamic doctrine of necessity, permitting an otherwise prohibited action when no permissible alternative is available; applied in Takaful where no re-Takaful capacity exists. [Ch. 29]
Family Takaful: The Shari’ah-compliant equivalent of life insurance, providing death and disability protection through a mutual contribution and shared risk structure. [Ch. 29]
Fatwa: A formal legal opinion issued by an Islamic scholar or Shari’ah board on a matter of Islamic law.
Fiqh Muamalat: Islamic commercial jurisprudence; the branch of Islamic law governing commercial transactions, including insurance. [Ch. 29]
Gharar: Excessive uncertainty or ambiguity in a contract; one of the three principal Shari’ah objections to conventional insurance. [Ch. 29]
General Takaful: The Shari’ah-compliant equivalent of general insurance, covering property, motor, and casualty risks for annual terms. [Ch. 29]
IFSB: Islamic Financial Services Board; the international prudential standard-setting body for Takaful and Islamic finance. [Ch. 29]
Ijara: An Islamic leasing structure; used in Federal Government Sukuk issuances where assets are sold and leased back. [Ch. 29]
Maysir: Gambling or speculative gain; one of the three Shari’ah objections to conventional insurance. [Ch. 29]
Mudarabah: An Islamic profit-sharing contract in which one party provides capital and the other provides management skill; used in the Mudarabah Takaful model. [Ch. 29]
Participants’ Risk Account (PRA): The collective Takaful mutual fund into which Tabaru’ contributions are pooled and from which claims are paid. [Ch. 29]
Participants’ Special Account (PSA): The individual savings account within a Family Takaful plan, belonging to the participant and invested in Shari’ah-compliant instruments. [Ch. 29]
Qard Hassan: An interest-free loan; in Takaful, the operator may provide a Qard Hassan to cover a PRA deficit, to be repaid from future surpluses. [Ch. 29]
Re-Takaful: The Takaful equivalent of reinsurance, based on mutual contribution principles. [Ch. 29]
Riba: Interest or usury; the Islamic prohibition on earning or paying interest, making conventional insurance investment Shari’ah-impermissible. [Ch. 29]
Shari’ah: Islamic law derived from the Qur’an, Sunnah, scholarly consensus, and analogical reasoning. [Ch. 29]
Shari’ah Supervisory Board (SSB): The independent body of Islamic scholars certifying the Shari’ah compliance of a Takaful operator’s products, investments, and operations. [Ch. 29]
Sukuk: Islamic bonds structured around asset-backed returns rather than interest; the primary Shari’ah-compliant fixed-income instrument for Takaful funds. [Ch. 29]
Tabaru’: An Islamic donation or charitable contribution; Takaful participants make Tabaru’ contributions to the mutual fund rather than paying premiums for a contractual benefit. [Ch. 29]
Takaful: Islamic insurance based on mutual contribution, shared risk, and Shari’ah-compliant investment. [Ch. 29]
Takaful Window: A ring-fenced Takaful operation within a conventional insurer’s corporate structure, with strict fund separation and its own SSB. [Ch. 29]
Wakalah: An Islamic agency contract in which one party acts as agent for another for a defined fee; the dominant Takaful operating model in Nigeria. [Ch. 29]
Waqf: An Islamic endowment dedicated to a charitable purpose; used as a Takaful fund structure in the Waqf model. [Ch. 29]

blocks.title: Section 14: Health Insurance and Group Employee Benefits

blocks.h: Health insurance models, HMO terminology, and employee benefit products.
Accidental Death Benefit (ADB): A group life rider paying an additional benefit if death is caused by an accident. [Ch. 30]
Benefit Schedule: The document listing the covered services and their limits in a health insurance plan. [Ch. 32]
Capitation: A payment model in which the HMO pays providers a fixed amount per enrolled member per month regardless of services utilised. [Ch. 32]
Claims Loss Ratio (Health): Total health claims incurred as a percentage of total premium earned; the primary health insurance performance metric. [Ch. 32]
Co-payment: The fixed amount paid by the insured at the point of service, shared with the insurer as a moral hazard management tool. [Ch. 32]
Corporate Employee Benefit (EB): A comprehensive package of insurance and savings products provided by an employer to its employees, including group life, health, and pension. [Ch. 30]
Critical Illness Benefit (CIB): A group life or standalone rider paying a lump sum on diagnosis of a defined critical illness. [Ch. 30]
Deductible: The amount the insured must pay out-of-pocket before the insurer covers remaining costs; more common in indemnity plans. [Ch. 32]
Dependant: A family member (spouse, child) covered under an employee’s health insurance plan.
Disease Management Programme: A structured intervention managing enrollees with chronic conditions to prevent expensive acute events and reduce claims costs. [Ch. 32]
Employee Value Proposition (EVP): The total package offered by an employer to attract and retain employees, including insurance and pension benefits. [Ch. 35]
Employer Group Life: Group life insurance provided by an employer to its employees; mandatory under the Pension Reform Act 2014 at a minimum of 3× annual emoluments. [Ch. 30]
Exclusion (Health): Conditions or circumstances not covered under a health insurance plan. [Ch. 32]
Fee-for-Service (FFS): A health insurance payment model in which providers are paid a defined fee per service rendered. [Ch. 32]
Free Cover Limit (Group Life): The sum assured per member provided without individual medical evidence in a group scheme. [Ch. 30]
Group Life Insurance: Life insurance covering all eligible employees of an employer under a single master policy. [Ch. 30]
HMO (Health Maintenance Organisation): An NHIA-licensed organisation providing defined health services to enrollees for a fixed capitation premium. [Ch. 32]
Indemnity Health Insurance: Health insurance reimbursing actual costs at any provider, without network restriction. [Ch. 32]
Medical Cost Inflation: The rate of increase in healthcare costs, typically exceeding general CPI; a critical risk in health insurance pricing. [Ch. 32]
NHIA (National Health Insurance Authority): The federal body responsible for licensing and supervising HMOs and working toward universal health coverage under the NHIA Act 2022. [Ch. 32]
Outpatient Care: Medical treatment that does not require overnight hospital admission. [Ch. 32]
Permanent Disability Benefit (PDB): A rider paying a lump sum if the insured employee becomes permanently unable to work. [Ch. 30]
Pre-Authorisation: The insurer’s advance approval for a defined healthcare service, required before the service is provided. [Ch. 32]
Pre-existing Condition: A health condition that existed before the insurance coverage commenced; typically subject to a waiting period or exclusion. [Ch. 32]
Provider Network: The hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies contracted by the HMO to provide services to enrollees. [Ch. 32]
Waiting Period (Health): A defined period after enrolment during which certain benefits (particularly for pre-existing conditions or maternity) are not payable. [Ch. 32]
CPS, PFA, annuity, and pension product terminology.
Accumulation Phase: The period during which an RSA holder or pension plan participant makes contributions and builds up their retirement fund. [Ch. 31]
Annuitant: The person receiving income payments under a life annuity. [Ch. 31]
Bulk Purchase Annuity (BPA): A transaction in which a defined benefit pension scheme transfers its pension payment obligations to a life insurer. [Ch. 31]
Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS): Nigeria’s mandatory defined-contribution pension system, established under the Pension Reform Act 2004 and reformed in 2014. [Ch. 33]
Decumulation Phase: The retirement period during which accumulated pension savings are converted into income, either through a Retirement Life Annuity or Programmed Withdrawal. [Ch. 31]
Defined Benefit (DB) Scheme: A pension arrangement in which the employer promises a defined retirement benefit based on salary and years of service. [Ch. 33]
Defined Contribution (DC) Scheme: A pension arrangement in which contributions are defined but the retirement benefit depends on accumulated fund performance; the CPS is a DC scheme. [Ch. 33]
Executive Pension Plan (EPP): An employer-sponsored supplementary pension for senior executives. [Ch. 33]
Income Replacement Ratio (IRR): The proportion of pre-retirement income needed to maintain the retiree’s standard of living; typically targeted at 70–80%. [Ch. 25]
Joint Life Annuity: A life annuity that continues to pay a reduced income to the surviving spouse after the annuitant’s death. [Ch. 31]
Level Annuity: A life annuity paying the same nominal income throughout the annuitant’s life. [Ch. 31]
Longevity Risk (Pension): The risk that annuitants outlive the mortality assumption, requiring more years of income payments than priced for. [Ch. 31]
Lump Sum Withdrawal: The right of an RSA holder to withdraw up to 25% of their RSA balance before converting the remainder to an annuity or PW. [Ch. 31]
National Pension Commission (PenCom): The federal regulator of Nigeria’s pension system, licensing PFAs and PFCs and supervising the RLA market. [Ch. 33]
Pension Fund Administrator (PFA): A PenCom-licensed company managing individual RSA contributions and investments. [Ch. 33]
Pension Fund Custodian (PFC): A PenCom-licensed institution physically holding and safeguarding RSA assets. [Ch. 33]
Pension Reform Act 2014: The primary legislation governing the Nigerian CPS, mandatory group life, RLA framework, and PFA licensing. [Ch. 33]
Personal Pension Plan (PPP): A long-term savings and insurance product for self-employed individuals outside the mandatory CPS. [Ch. 33]
Programmed Withdrawal (PW): The CPS alternative to the RLA, in which the RSA balance remains invested by the PFA and the holder draws a defined monthly income. [Ch. 31]
Retirement Life Annuity (RLA): The immediate life annuity purchased with RSA funds, providing guaranteed lifetime income. [Ch. 31]
Retirement Savings Account (RSA): The individual pension savings account held by each CPS contributor, managed by a PFA. [Ch. 33]
Succession Planning (Pension): The arrangement for managing RSA balances and pension benefits in the event of the RSA holder’s death before retirement. [Ch. 25]
Transitional Pension: Pension benefit payable to employees with service under pre-CPS DB schemes at the time of the 2004 transition. [Ch. 33]
Vesting: The process by which an employee’s right to employer pension contributions or deferred compensation becomes unconditional. [Ch. 33]
Voluntary Contribution (VC): An above-minimum, tax-deductible RSA contribution available to CPS members and the self-employed. [Ch. 33]
Voluntary RSA: An RSA opened specifically for voluntary contributions by individuals outside mandatory CPS coverage. [Ch. 33]

blocks.title: Section 16: Corporate Governance and Organisational Terms

blocks.h: Board governance, management structure, and organisational design terminology.
Audit Committee: The Board committee responsible for overseeing the integrity of financial statements and the internal and external audit functions. [Ch. 34]
Balanced Scorecard: A strategic performance measurement framework translating strategy into objectives across financial, customer, process, and learning perspectives. [Ch. 27]
Board Charter: The foundational governance document defining the Board’s role, composition, authority, and relationship with management. [Ch. 34]
CEO (Chief Executive Officer): See MD/CEO.
CFO (Chief Financial Officer): The senior executive responsible for financial management, reporting, investment, and NAICOM statutory filing. [Ch. 34]
CRO (Chief Risk Officer): The senior executive responsible for the ERM framework, ORSA, and monitoring material risks, with direct Board access. [Ch. 34]
Code of Conduct: The behavioural standards document for directors, executives, and employees. [Ch. 35]
